nameStory: The 'red buffalo-bur' name comes from its bright red fruits and the dense covering of sharp prickles that make it as formidable as a buffalo's tough hide. The 'bur' part refers to those same spiny structures that stick to clothing and fur, helping the plant spread its seeds. It's also called the 'fire-and-ice plant' because of its fiery red exterior contrasting with the cool yellow flesh inside.
description: Red buffalo-bur is a spiny annual plant in the nightshade family, closely related to tomatoes and potatoes. The entire plant is covered in sharp prickles that make it look like nature's barbed wire. It produces small red fruits about the size of cherry tomatoes that grow inside green, spiny husks. This South American native is extremely rare in New England, with only one recorded observation in the region.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Small red berries enclosed in spiny green husks, ripening to easily detach from stems when ready. The fruit has bright red skin with yellow flesh inside and tastes like sour cherries mixed with tomato.

idTips.label: Prickles
idTips.description: Sharp, needle-like prickles cover stems, leaves, and fruit husks. These feel genuinely dangerous to touch and will easily pierce clothing and skin.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Five-petaled flowers typical of nightshades, usually white or pale purple. They have the classic star shape with prominent yellow centers that tomato gardeners would recognize.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply lobed leaves with spiny prickles along the veins and stems. The leaf shape is somewhat similar to tomato leaves but much more heavily defended.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Sprawling annual that can form dense, impenetrable patches. The entire plant has a wild, unkempt appearance and creates natural barriers that animals avoid.

habitat: This species is not established in New England and has been found only once in the region, likely as an escape from cultivation or accidental introduction. In its native range, it prefers disturbed soils and waste areas. Given New England's climate, it would most likely appear in warm, sunny locations with well-drained soil if it were to establish.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in late spring when soil warms. Young plants begin developing their characteristic prickly armor as they establish.
seasonality.summer: Flowering occurs in mid to late summer with small white or pale purple star-shaped blooms. The plant reaches full size and prickliness during hot weather.
seasonality.fall: Fruits ripen to bright red in early fall and become easily detachable from stems when mature. The spiny husks split open to reveal the colorful berries inside.
seasonality.winter: As an annual, the plant dies with first frost, leaving behind dried stems and scattered seeds for potential spring germination.

funFact: This fierce-looking plant is actually used as a bodyguard for potato crops! Farmers deliberately plant it near potatoes because it attracts and traps destructive nematodes that would otherwise attack the potato roots, essentially sacrificing itself to protect the cash crop.
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with Carolina horsenettle, another spiny nightshade, but red buffalo-bur has much more elaborate spiny husks around its fruits and the fruits are distinctly red rather than yellow or orange. The prickles on red buffalo-bur are also more numerous and vicious-looking.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its fearsome appearance, red buffalo-bur produces edible fruits that are considered a delicacy in South America, where it's called 'litchi tomato.' However, like all nightshades, the leaves and stems contain toxic compounds and should never be eaten.
compareHints: Unlike other nightshades in New England, red buffalo-bur is the most heavily armed with prickles covering every surface. Carolina horsenettle has some spines but nothing like this species' full-body armor. The fruit's spiny husk is also unique among regional nightshades - bittersweet nightshade has smooth red berries, and black nightshades have dark berries without any protective covering.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike other nightshades in New England, bittersweet nightshade is the only one that grows as a climbing vine with purple flowers.
Among New England's nightshades, Carolina horsenettle is the only one covered in sharp prickles, making it instantly recognizable.
Unlike bittersweet nightshade which has purple flowers and grows as a climbing vine, eastern black nightshade has white flowers and grows as a low bushy annual.
Among its nightshade relatives in New England, tomato is easily distinguished by its large, edible red fruit and cultivation in gardens.
Among New England nightshades, buffalo-bur is unmistakable due to its extreme spininess - no other Solanum species is nearly as heavily armed with spines.
Black nightshade differs from its cousin bittersweet nightshade by being much smaller and having white flowers instead of purple ones with swept-back petals.
Unlike its nightshade relatives, potato has compound leaves rather than simple ones, and produces edible underground tubers.
Hairy nightshade differs from eastern black nightshade by its distinctly hairy stems and leaves (black nightshade is mostly smooth).

Green nightshade stands apart from its New England nightshade relatives primarily by its persistently green, glossy berries - eastern black nightshade and black nightshade both produce dark purple-black berries when ripe, while bittersweet nightshade produces bright red berries.
Unlike its wild nightshade relatives that grow as weeds in New England, cultivated eggplant is much larger in all aspects - bigger leaves, bigger flowers, and dramatically bigger fruits.

Garden huckleberry differs from other nightshades in New England by its drooping clusters of dark berries and relatively benign nature – unlike bittersweet nightshade with its bright red berries, or the more weedy black nightshade species.
